item.title: GOP is touting tax cuts to keep Ohio and Congress red. Voters aren't sold.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
MEDINA, Ohio – On a cold fall Saturday morning, Kristin Shepard carried a homemade sign with the letters V-O-T-E to the historic Public Square in this Republican-leaning area. She was asking people to get to the ballot box, like she did, with early voting underway. But fewer people were around than she expected. Shepard, 78, has been surprised by the influx of ads from Republicans during this election, including one she remembered about a bartender who praised not having to pay taxes on the tips she earned, referencing a provision in the Republicans’ sweeping tax cut legislation that President Donald Trump signed into law in the summer of 2025. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Shepard said that the GOP’s signature legislative achievement of the last two years has had no material impact on her own life. She is more concerned about Trump’s other policies. She voted for Democrats. “We’re in a war that never should have been started. We have tariffs that are hurting farmers, small-business people. I could go on and on,” said Shepard, a Medina resident who has been turned off by Trump. “And I will tell you, I voted Republican more in my life than I voted Democrat.” Republicans have bombarded Ohioans with ads with $19 million spent on competitive races through Oct. 12, intended to sell voters on the tax law that had been called the One Big Beautiful Bill. But the message is struggling to connect with voters amid anxiety over tariffs and the war with Iran, which have pushed up prices for everyday products. The ad blitz, the most spent on the topic in any state with competitive races, is aimed at bolstering vulnerable GOP candidates in a state that was considered safely Republican for the better part of the last decade. Yet, two dozen Ohio voters across Medina and Mahoning and counties told The Washington Post the ads were not making them feel any better about Republicans. The tax package was the most significant piece of legislation Republicans passed in the 119th Congress, as slim majorities in both chambers and fractious divisions within the party derailed much of the other Trump policy priorities, leaving the GOP with little else to tout on the campaign trail. Ariel Bly, a 33-year-old resident of Medina, Ohio, said the elimination of taxes on tips has been particularly helpful to friends of hers. But Bly, a swing voter who has supported candidates from both major parties, said she plans to vote mostly Democratic in the election as she is “slightly worried” about the economy. Bly said she is “not hugely thrilled” about Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican who was appointed to fill JD Vance’s seat after he became vice president and is now running for a full term , or his opponent Sherrod Brown, the former Democratic senator who lost his reelection bid in 2024, the same year that Trump won the state by 11 points. Bly said given her concerns about the direction of the country, she will most likely cast her vote for Brown. Recent polls show the two candidates locked in a tight race. An October survey of likely voters by Bowling Green State University and YouGov found that 48 percent of respondents said they would vote for Brown compared with 42 percent who said they would support Husted. Other recent polls have found the race closer. The outcome of the Senate race could be key to whether Republicans hold the majority in the chamber. That race, and another four Ohio U.S. House seats, are currently considered competitive by the Cook Political Report. The Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll found 58 percent of likely voters saying they disapprove of Trump’s job as president and 46 percent saying their personal economic situation has gotten worse over the past year. While Trump is not on the ballot in the midterm election, his performance looms large over vulnerable candidates like Husted. One $6 million ad, which has aired more than 10,000 times as of Oct. 12, promotes some of the key elements of the Republicans’ sweeping tax cuts package. It says Husted has supported ending taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security, plus a $200 million investment in rural hospitals. Republicans have rebranded the bill they once referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill, changing the name to the “Working Family Tax Cuts Act” in an effort to focus messaging around the tax breaks. The $3.4 trillion package extended the individual income tax cuts from Trump’s first term, created new tax breaks for business and increased the cap on federal deductions for state and local taxes. It also enacted new benefits Trump promised during his 2024 campaign, including the reduction of taxes on tips and overtime pay through 2028. The law also included cuts to safety net programs, including Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. Nationwide, Republicans spent $91 million ads touting the tax break legislation in competitive races, according to an analysis by The Post, although the ads don’t mention the bill by its original name. Instead, the ads tend to refer to specific provisions from the bill, such as no tax on tips and overtime. At a campaign stop at the Mahoning County Republican Party Headquarters in Boardman, Ohio, on Thursday, Husted told reporters his final pitch to voters centers on comparing Brown’s record with his own, including his support of the tax cuts. When asked about how voters have reacted to the Working Families Tax Cuts Act on the campaign trail, Husted said they “appreciate it greatly.” “I’ve talked to delivery drivers and servers and people who have said this is great. It’s helped them pay off student loans, pay off cars, do things like that with the extra money they’re saving,” Husted said. “I talked to a young man in Findlay, Ohio, who told me that he was going to dedicate his year to working overtime, 55 hours a week, and the money that he would save from that alone would allow him to put a down payment on his first home.” Drew Carchedi, a 45-year-old resident of Poland, Ohio, who attended Husted’s campaign event said the tax cuts and benefits for small businesses were particularly helpful. Tom McCabe, chair of the Republican Party in Mahoning County, said the messaging on the Working Family Tax Cuts Act plays well in this area home to many blue-collar workers. Mahoning County used to be more Democratic but has trended red over the last decade. Trump won the county in 2016, the first Republican presidential candidate to do so since 1972. McCabe said he thinks messaging on the tax cuts have been crucial to energizing voters in the county, which he expects Republicans to carry again in the Nov. 3 election, though he did recognize that the issues of inflation and climbing gas prices weigh heavy on voters. “I think people have short term memories of what we were paying for bread and eggs four years ago under Biden,” McCabe said. “It’s always the pocketbook issues at the end of the day, but I think Trump’s economics policies have resonated here.” But back in Medina, Eric Larson, a 50-year-old resident of Montville Township, Ohio, was less than convinced that the tax cuts had done anything for him. Larson was handing out fliers at the Public Square in support of Ohio Democrats. The flier read: “SHERROD BROWN AND AMY ACTON WILL FIGHT TO LOWER COSTS FOR WORKING FAMILIES.” Acton is currently running for governor against Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate. The race is also rated as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. Larson said he had not always supported Democrats. He was previously registered as a Republican and has a history of splitting his ticket, voting for candidates from both major parties in the same election. But this year, he said he’s voting Democrats up and down the ballot. “I have a handful of friends who still consider themselves Republicans, they can’t even vote for this stuff,” Larson said. - - - Graphics: In Senate races, Ohio leads in ad spending on the 2025 tax and spending law Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/20/inside-gops-effort-keep-ohio-red-touting-tax-cuts-no-tax-tips/

item.title: U.S. is reportedly nearing a deal with Russia to free multiple jailed Americans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is closing in on a deal with Moscow that would see multiple Americans released from detention in Russia, two U.S. officials and another source familiar with the matter tell ABC News. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner have been leading the negotiations, which are said to be in the final stages, according to the sources. With Gilman's release from Russia, families of other detained Americans hope their relatives will be next They add that the talks have centered on freeing Stephen Hubbard , a 72-year-old retired teacher who is the only American held in Russia officially designated as wrongfully detained by the State Department, as well as several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration said it believes are dubious charges. Moscow City Court Press Service via AP - PHOTO: In this Oct. 7, 2024, file photo released by the Moscow City Court Press Service, Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen accused of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine against Russia stands in a glass cage during a court session in Moscow. However, officials caution that while the terms of the arrangement are coming into focus, nothing has been finalized and it’s still possible it won’t materialize or that its scope will change. News of the potential deal comes as Witkoff is expected to travel to Moscow this week following his meeting with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, Norway, one official said. On Monday, Trump spoke about his dealings with Russia, saying he was "trying to get a hostage that the country has been after for a long time," presumably referring to Hubbard. "Let's see what happens," Trump said. "That'll be soon." Trump signs order waiving Graham Act sanctions on Russia, drawing backlash from some lawmakers and Zelenskyy On Tuesday, Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov was asked about a potential prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. "Dialogue on all these issues is ongoing through intelligence service channels," he said. Ryabkov added that Hubbard's name was "certainly familiar," but said he had "nothing to report" on the matter. Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this Jan. 10, 2022, file photo, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov looks on during a press conference following talks with US counterpart on soaring tensions over Ukraine, in Geneva. The White House declined to comment on the matter. It's not clear what Russia might receive in exchange for releasing U.S. citizens. However, Trump has made multiple policy decisions viewed as favorable to Moscow in recent days, including waiving newly imposed sanctions targeting Russian officials and oligarchs mandated by a bill Trump signed into law last month after it passed by wide margins in Congress. Trump has also increased pressure on Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian energy sites. There are currently at least eight Americans in Russian custody. item.title: Senate Democrats air first ad in Mississippi as midterm optimism grows
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats' top campaign spending group is wading into Mississippi's U.S. Senate race for the first time this year, an aggressive move in a deep-red state that signals a party on the offensive as Republicans look to protect a slim majority. The Senate Majority PAC, aligned with Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, will spend $1.2 million on a new television advertisement to boost Scott Colom , a district attorney, in his campaign against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. The ad, first disclosed to The Associated Press, is set to start Wednesday and run through Election Day. “Senate Majority PAC has been watching this race closely, and it is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” group spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement. With just two weeks to go in the race, it's unclear what impact the ad will have in a matchup that's been set since Colom won a March primary . Still, it's a substantial investment in a race that's seen only about $8 million in total spending, with Colom outspending Hyde-Smith nearly $4.6 million to $3.2 million, according to AdImpact. Jake Monssen, campaign manager for Hyde-Smith, noted that the spending was coming late in the race. “Team Cindy is confident that voters will reject this radical agenda at the ballot box on November 3rd,” he said. Democrats believe Hyde-Smith is vulnerable Hyde-Smith, first appointed and then elected in 2018 , is running for reelection in a state Republicans have long dominated. In the 2024 presidential race, Republican Donald Trump won Mississippi by nearly 23 percentage points over Democrat Kamala Harris, and a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate race in the state since 1982. However, some Democrats believe Hyde-Smith is vulnerable, and she underperformed Trump by 6 percentage points in 2020 , the year he lost his White House reelection bid to Democrat Joe Biden. The television ad touts Colom's time as district attorney, while labeling Hyde-Smith a “do-nothing” senator. “A decade in power, Hyde-Smith hasn’t passed one piece of legislation, but she did vote to kick people off Medicaid,” a narrator says in the ad, which will run on television stations statewide alongside a digital campaign. Harris and other high-profile Democrats have raced to campaign with Colom Colom's campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, said that the contest against an incumbent senator is competitive because “thousands of Mississippians volunteered and chipped in.” “We clearly have the resources and momentum to win,” Henderson said in a statement. Colom has raised Democratic hopes in a year when electoral winds are at their backs. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock was the latest high-profile Democrat to campaign with Colom last week, and Harris, who was Biden's vice president, is set to rally with Colom on Thursday. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and were expected to face a friendlier map this year with fewer seats to defend. But high costs and gas prices amid an unpopular war in Iran under a Republican president have made Democrats optimistic, with the Senate Majority PAC spending its final weeks investing in conservative territory . It's already announced spending in Kansas , where megachurch pastor and Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton is trying to unseat Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. Colom would be his state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, the 12-year period after the U.S. Civil War when the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments were adopted. Some Democrats have criticized national groups for not spending more in Southern states like Mississippi . “I worry, to be very honest, that Democrats are missing a real opportunity to invest in a serious and sustained way in the South,” Warnock said Sunday on NBC’s ”Meet the Press." This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/senate-democrats-launch-first-ad-160013215.html

item.title: Russia, sensing victory, cheers Trump's latest shift against Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Kremlin is counting the Trump administration’s latest turn against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as a major triumph and, coupled with political upheaval in Europe, a sign that Western support for Ukraine is finally crumbling. In the 10 days since Vladimir Putin last spoke by telephone with the American president, Donald Trump has announced a sanctions waiver for Russian diesel supplies to the global market, throttled Ukraine’s access to vital battlefield satellite systems, put sweeping new sanctions against Russian on hold, as well as moved even more firmly to Russia’s side by calling for Zelensky’s ouster and holding up supplies of critical interceptor missiles. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. On Monday, Trump blasted the Ukrainian president again, saying it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.” The stakes seem higher than ever. Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is set to travel to Oslo on Tuesday to meet Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is expected to participate via video link. “The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path,” Store said. Zelensky said on Sunday that if Washington aligned with Russia, Ukraine would not survive. “If the United States will support Putin - it’s unbelievable, it’s a tragedy,” he told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday. “If these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail. And we will not be able to stand.” While the European leaders and Zelensky might hope to use the Oslo meeting to steer the Trump administration to a tougher stance against Moscow, Kremlin officials have been crowing that victory over Ukraine is on the horizon, and that Trump’s recent moves are steps toward an ever-closer alignment between Washington and Moscow. Trump’s recent ratcheting-up of pressure on Zelensky could mean the U.S. president is again seeking to strong-arm the Ukrainian leader into a deal on terms favorable to Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that Witkoff is expected to brief Putin following the Oslo talks. Earlier, Peskov said Ukraine’s recent resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries - in defiance of Trump’s demands - showed Zelensky’s administration in its death throes. “Some final signs of agony are being observed,” Peskov said. “The Kyiv regime is resisting. But this cannot change the course of events.” “Checkmate,” Kremlin special envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted triumphantly. In Moscow, members of the Russian elite said that Putin, a former KGB officer, once again managed to turn the U.S. president. Putin has decades of experience charming and manipulating foreign leaders, and has demonstrated a consistent ability to flatter Trump and pull him on side, analysts and officials said. This time, they said, the Russian leader preyed on Trump’s fears over low approval ratings and sky-high energy prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, offering a deal on Russian diesel fuel that will supply just a fraction of America’s daily consumption and have no impact on prices. On Friday, the average U.S. diesel price continued to climb to $6.33 per gallon, an increase of about 5 cents per gallon from the previous week. “Russia’s leaders have achieved a certain political victory,” said a Russian academic close to senior Russian diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy. “All this happened after their telephone call. Probably Putin was able to convince Trump.” Putin, the academic added, “probably conducted this conversation very professionally and prepared his arguments well.” Mikhail Khodorkovsky, once Russia’s richest man and now an opposition leader in exile, said recent events followed a pattern in Putin’s relations with Trump. “I am absolutely convinced that they believe that they managed to take advantage, as they always do; they are opportunists,” Khodorkovsky said. “In this case, they believe they have waited for the moment of Trump’s additional weakness and [taken] advantage of it.” “For Putin, everything that is happening today are signs of the West’s weakness,” he said. Dmitriev, the special envoy, and other Russian officials hailed the diesel deal and Trump’s waiving of tough sanctions that were to be imposed under a bill adopted in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, a firm GOP supporter of Ukraine, as steps toward broader Russia-U.S. economic cooperation. Historically, Russia and the U.S. have never been big economic partners, with Russia exporting little of interest to the U.S. market. “There is a whole range of economic and investment projects being discussed with the American side that will be implemented,” Dmitriev told a Russian energy forum last week. “Our list of projects being discussed with the American side also includes various projects in the Arctic, energy projects, LNG [liquefied natural gas] projects and other areas.” “More and more Americans, including within the administration, understand that sanctions harm the United States itself,” he added. In July - after years of Putin refusing to drop his maximalist demands in Ukraine - Trump finally seemed to side with Zelensky, telling reporters he was doing “an amazing job” and even backing Ukraine’s deep strikes on Russian oil refineries. “It’s an escalation, but it’s also an escalation that can help lead to an end” of the war, Trump said. But as the U.S. conflict with Iran dragged on, keeping upward pressure on global oil prices, and as the midterm elections drew ever nearer, the Trump administration suddenly turned again. After an Aug. 31 meeting with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a Group of 20 event in Asheville, North Carolina, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries as the reason for surging fuel prices - rather than the war in Iran. It was then easy for Putin to recruit Trump into sharing that viewpoint, some observers said. “The simplest explanation is that Trump was simply interested in having a talking point for the midterms on diesel, that he has a deal to lower it, said Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for Europe during George W. Bush’s administration. “I think it is just Trump lashing out because he’s feeling cornered and unhappy with the midterms, and Zelensky stood in his way,” Fried said, especially after Zelensky publicly derided Trump as “weak” after he announced the diesel deal. “Trump then extended his frustration to add pressure and try to force a settlement based on a great power deal with Putin, who is skilled at playing his more gullible interlocutors,” he said. That Trump and Putin share a view that strongmen should dominate a world divided into spheres of influence made it even easier for Putin, Fried added. “Trump appears to have been attracted to this view for decades,” he said. “And therefore, Ukraine is expendable on strategic grounds, in Trump’s view, and it was standing in the way of a perfectly good campaign talking point.” Trump’s latest swing toward Putin was hardly surprising, said a former senior U.S. intelligence official. “It almost doesn’t matter what he says, because Trump just seems like he’s very eager. He’s a very receptive audience,” the former intelligence official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. “If you look at the longer-term trends, he has clearly a preference for Putin over Zelensky, and that transcends any kind of temporary relaxation of the tensions that he has with Zelensky.” “He likes strong authoritarian leaders,” the official said. “And deep down, there is this underlying belief on his part that Ukraine cannot win this war, that Russia is bigger, Russia is stronger, Russia is going to crush Ukraine if that’s what it takes.” Signs point to Trump seeking to strong-arm Ukraine into a deal by December, when Trump has invited Putin to join him at the G-20 leaders’ summit in Miami, said Andrew Weiss, a Russian expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington. “The only way I can explain it is that it’s connected to the milestones leading up to the meeting of the G-20 in December,” Weiss said. “I feel like what’s going on here is not really about diesel or refinery long-range strikes. It’s really about Trump thinking that he can push the Ukrainians into some sort of political settlement.” The Russians have “tried to use the administration as a battering ram to get the Ukrainians to surrender Donbas,” Weiss said, referring to the swath of eastern Ukraine coveted by Putin. “But then that only opens up a subsequent conversation about constraints on Ukrainian military capabilities,” he added, or other underlying Russian demands. “The administration has repeatedly misdiagnosed what the Russians want, and the Russians don’t make that easy because they don’t say exactly what they want.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/20/russia-sensing-victory-cheers-trumps-latest-shift-against-ukraine/

item.title: States are preparing for an unusual election threat from the federal government
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A small group of U.S. national security officials has been discreetly advising state governments and congressional lawmakers on how to prepare for the possibility that the Trump administration will attempt to interfere in November's midterm elections, according to people involved in the effort. The group includes about 10 current and former officials with experience in the Defense Department, some of whom have previously focused on countering authoritarianism abroad. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Their efforts are motivated not by political bias, they say, but a growing sense of alarm that President Donald Trump will harm American democracy by undermining the integrity of the vote to keep the Republican Party in power. Over the past several months, the group has consulted with officials from 10 states, including governors, election officials and members of the House and Senate from both political parties who share a fear of federal intervention, two people involved in the effort said. The effort, which has not been previously reported, focuses on states and jurisdictions where tightly contested races will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's presidency. Members of the group remain in contact with congressional staffs, and at least one state has continued to meet with them as it works to address potential vulnerabilities. "All of them have said we're concerned but we don't know what to do," one member of the group said of its meetings with lawmakers. "The outcome that we hope for is that states would be prepared for any contingencies should they arise," the person continued. This report is based on interviews, conducted over several months, with two officials involved in the effort. They spoke on the condition of anonymity and that the lawmakers and state leaders with whom the group has met not be identified either, for fear of retaliation. The Washington Post also reviewed some of the documents the group prepared for its meetings. Trump has long claimed that a "deep state" of government officials is working to undermine his presidency. Since returning to office, he has undertaken an expansive effort to fire career civil servants and solicit political loyalty from the bureaucracy. Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, dismissed the group's concerns and blamed Democrats for not supporting stricter election laws. The Trump administration, she said in a statement, "is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion." The president, Bis added, "is making clear that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable." In their discussions ahead of the midterms, the national security officials have detailed ways the Trump administration could use its federal powers to sway the upcoming vote, covering categories that include legal and illegal activity. Among their concerns are that the administration could deploy troops or immigration agents to polling stations or seek to nullify results based on claims of voter fraud. Their meetings with lawmakers have mainly focused on raising awareness, especially among Republicans, of the potential for interference and on counseling them to be prepared to publicly oppose any such efforts. With state governments, they've focused more on how to harden election protocols that could be exploited by the federal government, the two members of the group said. Their warnings are based on personal analysis of the administration's activities and public statements made by the president and his allies - not access to specific government intelligence or information to which they have access because of their positions within federal agencies, members of the group said. They described the meetings as a way to help state and federal officials secure the election and emphasized that their work has occurred outside of their official capacity as government employees. Still, their efforts indicate an extraordinary level of concern that Trump may use his authority to influence the election or challenge the results, similar to his extended campaign to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election that culminated with a raid on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. Trump's approval rating is at record lows only weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, with voters frustrated about the cost of living and the war in Iran. Democrats appear likely to flip the House and possibly the Senate, and have vowed to intensify oversight of the administration if they regain power. Election officials, including some Republicans, have decried efforts by the Trump administration to assert federal control over a process that the Constitution entrusts to the states. Some GOP-led states, such as Utah, have refused to comply with the administration's efforts to access their voter rolls. "The threats that we're getting now are mostly from our own government," Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson told The Post earlier this month. In January, the FBI raided an election office in Fulton County, Georgia, and seized voting materials in an investigation tied to Trump's debunked claims of voter fraud in the 2020 election. Trump told the New York Times in an interview earlier this year that he regretted not having the National Guard seize voting machines during that race. As he has campaigned on behalf of Republicans, Trump has repeated his claims about the 2020 election and that Democrats are attempting mass voter fraud ahead of the midterms. In October, a group of nongovernmental organizations sued the administration, alleging that it unlawfully collected voting data from 47 states. Throughout the year, he has unsuccessfully urged Congress to pass an election security bill - the SAVE America Act - that would give the federal government more authority over the voting process. The GOP-controlled Senate has not done so, as passing the bill would require ending the chamber's 60-vote threshold known as the filibuster. Trump and some of his top Cabinet officials also have declined to rule out the possibility that they will send members of the military or immigration agents to polling stations, alarming Democrats. During a combative Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in late April, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was asked whether he would refuse a presidential order to deploy troops to the polls or to collect voting machines. He dismissed the question, posed by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), as a "hypothetical." When the committee's Republican chairman, Sen. Roger Wicker (Mississippi), urged Hegseth to provide a response, the secretary said, "I've never been ordered to do anything illegal, and I won't." In August, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, wrote to Slotkin and said that there were no plans to deploy troops to the polls or seize voting records. The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment. In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin declined to rule out the possibility of deploying immigration agents to the polls. Speaking to reporters, Mullin said that they would appear only if there were "specific threats" and that such agents wouldn't "patrol" voting sites. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said that Immigration and Customs Enforcement "is not planning operations targeting polling locations" and would only do so if an "active public safety threat endangered a polling location." At other times, Trump and other senior officials have attempted to use the powers of their office to sway voters to support Republicans. The president has promised voters a $5,000 reward if the GOP maintains its majority in Congress, and he has used taxpayer money to air campaign-style ads ahead of the midterms. The precautions some states are taking against potential federal interference in the midterms signal a radical departure from the threats that state governments normally focus on in an election year. Foreign actors such as China and Russia have long sought to influence or disrupt U.S. elections, and continue to do so ahead of the November midterms, the U.S. intelligence community has assessed. Tammy Patrick, the chief program officer at the National Association of Election Officials, said that over the past year the possibility of federal interference has become the dominant concern of election officials she has spoken to around the country. State and local officials, for example, have been rehearsing how to respond if a federal agent appears at a polling place to compel access to ballots or voting machines, she said. Other officials, Patrick said, have been concerned about moves the Trump administration has already taken. Since returning to office, Trump has pressured states, such as Indiana and Texas, to redraw their congressional maps to favor Republicans. His administration has also asked the Supreme Court to limit the availability of mail-in voting, a request the court has rejected. "All of these things," Patrick said, "are being done in the open." Patrick Marley contributed to this report. item.title: California residents accused by feds of voter fraud react with shock, confusion, anger
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Homeland Security Investigations officers leave a home after arresting a suspect accused of illegally registering to vote during a federal operation in Commerce on Monday. (Jae C. Hong / Associated Press) At the federal courthouse in downtown Los Angeles late Monday, several green card holders arrested in a crackdown on alleged California voter fraud expressed confusion over the charges — with some saying they had no recollection of registering to vote, as Trump administration officials accuse them of doing. Among them was Ana Domínguez, 60, a native of El Salvador living in Long Beach as a lawful permanent resident. Federal authorities accused her Monday of fraudulently registering to vote in July 2006 and then lying about it in her naturalization paperwork in March 2026. Domínguez said she did not have any memory of registering to vote. Another man accused of the same crimes as Domínguez said the same: He wasn’t aware of ever registering to vote, as federal prosecutors claimed he had. Both were among the 28 people charged with federal election-related crimes Monday, including fraudulent voter registration and making false statements in a naturalization application. Federal prosecutors and high-ranking Justice Department officials had touted the arrests during a news conference hours before as proof that California elections are corrupted by noncitizen voters — as President Trump has long alleged. For those charged in the Central District of California, voter registration and public records showed at least two individuals who shared the names of defendants were registered to vote as Republicans, two as Democrats, two as supporters of the Peace and Freedom Party and three with no party preference chosen. Read more: Feds arrest alleged noncitizen voters in California amid broader election fight with state State officials said the isolated instances of noncitizens voting, if accurate, are not evidence of widespread voter fraud. They also raised questions as to whether the charges could be trusted to be accurate — citing similar accusations being disproved elsewhere in the country. Election experts have said many instances of noncitizens registering to vote are a result of administrative error or confusion on the part of the immigrant — not intentional criminality. “We know from past experience that sometimes people register to vote accidentally, as when there is a mistake at the DMV,” Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law, wrote Monday in a blog post. “There is only a crime if the government can prove willful violations of federal law.” Four of the defendants charged Monday had initial court appearances later that afternoon. Beforehand, more than a dozen of their loved ones milled around the federal courthouse in downtown L.A., antsy and clearly worried. One woman, her baby and young daughter in tow, struggled to find the right courtroom. Another woman, Domínguez’s daughter, cried in the hallway as she waited for her mother’s case to get called up. When Domínguez moved to stand before the judge, she blew a kiss to her husband and daughter in the second row. She wore a black back brace and her legs were cuffed. A third defendant — Omar Muñoz, 72, a lawful permanent resident from Belize whose arrest at his home in Commerce was captured by photographers in images transmitted around the world — shuffled into a court room shackled at the waist, his feet cuffed, still wearing the red and black pajama pants he’d been arrested in. Homeland Security Investigations task force officers escort a suspect accused of illegally registering to vote to a processing facility in Los Angeles on Monday. (Jae C. Hong / Associated Press ) Muñoz was charged with fraudulently registering to vote in September 2019, and then voting in 2020, twice in 2022 and again in 2024. He is also accused of lying on his application to become a naturalized U.S. citizen, when he claimed to have never falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen in the past. In the courtroom, Muñoz held a hand over his heart as he waved to his family in the first row of the gallery. Hasen, the UCLA expert, wrote that the government’s blasting out images of Muñoz being arrested was clearly “meant to convey that the problem of noncitizen voting in California is both pervasive and serious, crimes that are undetected by willfully ignorant California election officials.” But the reality, he wrote, “is likely far different,” with voter fraud limited to isolated cases, some with less nefarious intent. First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said Monday that the cases represent strong federal work to ensure that noncitizens aren’t negating the votes of eligible U.S. voters — a problem he said California officials have refused to recognize despite federal authorities providing the proof. Essayli dismissed the idea that those charged may have been unaware of what they were doing. “You have to go out of your way to register to vote; it’s not something that just happens to you,” Essayli said. José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, a Mexican national and West Adams resident, appeared in court wearing a reflective vest with the name of a landscaping company, blue jeans and boots with the American flag on them. He’d been on his way to work when he was arrested. During the hearings, the defendants spoke only to acknowledge that they reviewed and understood the charges against them. In every case, the federal prosecutor said the government was not seeking detention. Read more: Big assertions, sharp exchanges, little clarity define DOJ election battle with California The magistrate judge ordered the four released on personal recognizance and said they were not required to be under supervision. They are all set to appear in court for a preliminary hearing Nov. 9. Their deputy federal public defenders did not respond to a request for comment. Lliani Orantes, Muñoz’s daughter and a nurse who was born in the U.S., said her father had been hauled out of the family home by federal authorities after they swarmed and cordoned off the block. She said the family was rushing to figure out what happened, including whether Muñoz could have been confused with younger relatives of the same name, including a U.S.-born son who is a registered voter. Orantes also expressed frustration with the handling of her father’s arrest — to which federal authorities had clearly alerted some media, who were brought along for the raid. She said that her father is recovering from cervical surgery, rotator cuff repair on a shoulder and a double knee replacement, and that he was pulled out of the family’s home “like he was a dog” as part of what she described as a “political ploy, an example used for the operation” — which federal authorities dubbed “Operation Protect the Vote.” “They’re trying to instill fear in society,” she said. “We have so much more in the world to be dealing with, do we really need to focus on these little things that could be taken care of in a different fashion? In a different way? Like, hey, somebody from immigration visit the home,” she said. Acting U.S. Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter speaks at a news conference Monday to announce charges against 28 people in California accused of illegally registering to vote as noncitizens. (David Butow / For The Times) California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta — who is defending the state and top election officials for the state and Los Angeles County against a lawsuit from the Justice Department alleging they are not treating alleged voter fraud by noncitizens seriously enough — said Monday that voting illegally is wrong and “one-off, isolated incidents” of it should be prosecuted. But Bonta denied that there is widespread voter fraud in the state, called 28 cases brought out of the 23 million registered voters in California a “drop in the bucket,” and said he’d be watching how those cases play out in court. “We’ll see what the facts show, and whether they’ll have to drop charges or whether they’ll be able to prosecute,” he said. About 3 p.m. Monday, the four defendants at the downtown courthouse were released and exited the courtroom, some to family members waiting in the hallway to hug them. Domínguez wiped away tears as she recounted her arrest, showing bruises on her wrists from the handcuffs. “They were accusing me of voter fraud since 2006,” she said. Domínguez said the accusations don’t even make sense considering she has never voted. “If I would have committed all those frauds about voting registration and whatever they’re saying, since 2006, wouldn’t you imagine that I would have been voting all these other years?” she asked. Read more: Justice Dept. sues California, seeks to stop state from counting 20,000 ballots In a visual presentation at their news conference, federal authorities alleged that 21 of the 28 people charged had actually voted. Domínguez was not one of them. Domínguez said she’s been a lawful permanent resident since the late 1980s, and that she applied for U.S. citizenship earlier this year. As part of the application process, she said she told an immigration agent that the only people registered to vote in her household were her husband, who previously became a U.S. citizen, and her daughter, who was born in the country. Since then, Domínguez said, she has just been waiting on the citizenship ceremony, “but it never came through.” Instead, she was arrested Monday when she was about to leave for work as an administrative assistant. “I never, ever in my entire life ... thought this would ever happen to me,” she said. Acting U.S. Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter stands next to a display showing photos of people charged with illegally registering to vote. (Jae C. Hong / Associated Press ) Muñoz and his family gathered outside the courthouse. Muñoz, who declined to comment on the charges against him, said he’d been up to have coffee early that morning when he heard the commotion outside. Agents said if he didn’t open the door, they’d break it down. He described seeing helicopters, at least eight cars and several agents from different agencies descending on his home, and recalled thinking, “What movie am I in?” “That’s a lot of money. Taxpayers paying for that,” he said. “They could have sent me a letter saying report to the court.” Muñoz — who said he came to the U.S. legally in 1975 and has “paid all my taxes” since — said he explained to the arresting agents that he’d had six surgeries recently and they “didn’t care.” He said he didn’t learn about the charges against him until four hours later. Muñoz’s son, Omar Muñoz Jr., questioned why federal agents didn’t take his father’s age and ailments into consideration. “We understand that there’s a procedure that has to be addressed at court. But 5 in the morning, handcuffed? It’s just the way everything was done, and what my mom had to go through. It’s not just an impact on my father’s health, but also on my mom,” he said. “There is a law, we understand that. But innocent until proven guilty.” Muñoz’s wife, Esmeralda, echoed her son’s questions about why so many agents were deployed to their home. “Seriously? All these people just to come for an elderly person,” she said she told a federal agent. “It’s unbelievable.” Times researcher Cary Schneider contributed to this report. item.title: Ohio governor candidate hits back after estranged mother appears in attack ad
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Dr. Amy Acton , the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, pushed back forcefully Tuesday against an unattributed ad circulating online in which her long-estranged mother calls her “a liar” and insinuates she has mental health issues. The ad began circulating overnight, just two weeks before Election Day. Acton, Ohio's former public health director , is in a tight race with Republican billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy , a 2024 presidential candidate who has benefited from spending on his behalf that has exceeded $120 million. The online ad, which first surfaced in a post by an Ohio political blogger, spread quickly across social media platforms. It does not include the “paid for” tag that is legally required to air on TV so viewers can know its source. It was not immediately clear who produced it or paid for it, or how it was accessed for posting. It also was not clear if Acton's mother was paid for the one-minute spot. Her last known telephone number has been disconnected. Acton suggested Ramaswamy was behind the ad. “I won’t normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I’m complaining about, who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse," she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio. She said Ramaswamy was accused of similar personal attacks during his run for the GOP presidential nomination: “This is a lifelong pattern with my opponent.” Ramaswamy’s campaign issued a statement that did not address whether he was responsible for the ad or disavow it. In the statement, campaign spokeswoman Connie Luck said Acton “has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of.” In a statement released by Acton's campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, said the two were removed from their mother Donna Arthur's custody as children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Acton has not seen Arthur, whose last known address was in Pennsylvania, since they were in a courtroom together in 1978. According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported his alleged conduct to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died. Stearns accused Ramaswamy of being behind the ad, saying the Republican had stooped "to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.” Acton's mother does not mention Ramaswamy's name in the ad, but she suggests that Acton has misrepresented her opponent and the time her family was homeless and living in a tent when she was a child __ an experience Stearns corroborates. ___ Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report. President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, a suburb of Wichita, on October 19. - Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images President Donald Trump on Monday used an antisemitic term that he has used publicly at least once before as he​ defended Kansas Sen. Trump invoked the term “Shylock” while defending Marshall’s​ suing more than 700 patients for outstanding medical bills during his time as an obstetrician-gynecologist, as first reported by The New York Times . “You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people, and they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” Trump said at a rally in Kansas. “If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law. To me, Shylock is somebody that’s a money lender at high rates,” Trump told reporters at the time. “I’ve never heard it that way, you view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.” The Anti-Defamation League — which last year condemned Trump’s use of the word — wrote Tuesday on X that the term was “rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype.” “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community,” the group wrote. Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, noted on X that Trump had previously been criticized publicly for using the term. “Tonight Trump yet again used the antisemitic ‘Shylock’ — a year after he was called out for doing so and claimed he didn’t know it was problematic,” she said. “Again: not an accident. He has consistently normalized antisemitic conspiracy theories and tropes.” In 2014 , former President Joe Biden apologized for using the word. item.title: GOP attacks on El-Sayed's Muslim faith come to a head in heated town hall exchange
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a campaign rally in Flint, Michigan, on October 18. - Katie McTiernan/Anadolu/Getty Images The Muslim Brotherhood has become a flashpoint in Michigan’s Senate race, with Republicans trying to cast Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror and El-Sayed arguing that he is being unfairly accused of the same “dual loyalties” that former Presidents John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama once were. El-Sayed this weekend denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement founded in Egypt in 1928 — first in a heated exchange with a voter, and later when speaking with reporters — after Republicans have sought to highlight his family’s ties to the group and his past comments about it. “I do want to talk about why they want to make this their closing argument,” El-Sayed told reporters after a rally Sunday in Flint. “They want to speak to a certain implicit dual loyalty. This has a long history in our politics, that notion that people might pray a little bit differently, have a dual loyalty. It was the same thing they did to JFK when he ran for president, the notion that because he was Catholic that he somehow had dual loyalties. They did the same thing to President Obama simply because his father was of Muslim origin, even though his father is an avowed Christian.” He added: “This is nothing new. This is what they do when they have no message about the real issues in people’s lives.” GOP attacks on El-Sayed Republicans have increasingly drawn attention to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith in the closing weeks of one of the most important Senate races on the 2026 midterm election map. President Donald Trump, at a campaign rally Friday night, referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and falsely declared that the Democratic former public health official is a “jihadist.” Those comments have become staples of recent Trump rallies and social media comments. El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, said Sunday on CNN that he has “never called him a terrorist” and said he does not “speak for the president.” But Rogers accused El-Sayed of aligning with the Muslim Brotherhood. The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist movement with global offshoots that once wielded significant political power in Egypt, where it was founded. The movement officially rejects the use of violent means to secure its goals. However, offshoots of the group have been linked to attacks in the past. Trump signed an executive order in November that initiated a process by which certain chapters or other subdivisions of the Muslim Brotherhood could be considered for designation as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. “You know, he wants to play the victim. This is not about that. This is about the way you think, not the way you pray,” Rogers told CNN’s Dana Bash. “This is about your ideology and how dangerous it is.” El-Sayed’s town hall exchange The GOP efforts to tie El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Islamic extremism, burst into the open this weekend at a town hall in Caro. An attendee repeatedly pressed El-Sayed about the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he had yet to hear the candidate reject the organization. “Abdul, will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?” the man shouted from the crowd. El-Sayed, after disavowing the movement, blasted the man for implicitly assuming his “dual loyalty.” “You assume … that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution,” El-Sayed said. He later added, “For me, that Constitution is the guiding light.” The audience member walked out after the exchange as the crowd cheered for El-Sayed. Family history scrutinized The GOP attacks come after old tweets from El-Sayed’s half-sister resurfaced online, including a post from 2012 in which she described having “an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.” El-Sayed has said he does not know what his mother was doing in Egypt during the 1970s, explaining he was 3 when his parents divorced and didn’t see his mother for years. He was primarily raised in Michigan by his father and stepmother. El-Sayed in 2012 also signed an open letter supporting then-Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who had been elected earlier that year with the support of the Muslim Brotherhood after the overthrow of the country’s authoritarian government. A year earlier, he penned a Huffington Post op-ed calling on the United States to support young Arab protesters in Egypt, and downplaying concerns that supporting democracy there would lead to Muslim Brotherhood control of the nation. During a recent debate, Rogers pointed out that El-Sayed’s mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a non-profit that the Treasury Department in 2004 designated as an organization supporting terrorism. “Are you going after my mom?” said El-Sayed. “I was going after that organization that was indicted for funneling money to Al Qaeda,” Rogers said. “Look, that’s your mom. My mom worked at a small chamber of commerce. I’ll put my mom up any day for that.” El-Sayed responded he is a “dad and a doctor” who wants to “get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for All.” He said Rogers “wants this to be about anything but his own record.” El-Sayed in recent days also addressed his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, being placed on the federal Terrorism Screening Database — a situation she challenged as part of a 2016 class action lawsuit . It’s not clear why Jukaku, who was once p resident of UCLA’s Muslim Student Association and is now a home-school teacher and writer in California , was added to the list. “She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off,” El-Sayed told Fox News when asked about his wife’s sister being placed on the terrorist watchlist, which was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001, attacks. “You’ve got this system where folks are guilty until proven innocent because they’ve got different kinds of names, because of the infrastructure that people like Mike Rogers set up.” CNN’s Jeff Zeleny and Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report. item.title: New details emerge about dad who stopped Oregon school shooter within minutes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More details have emerged about the "hero" bystander who intervened within minutes of a gunman opening fire at an elementary school in Oregon. Kaylub Giamanco, 36, fatally shot the 16-year-old gunman who killed four people at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Oct. 15. His actions "undoubtedly saved people," police said. Giamanco, a carpenter and father of two girls who attend Silver Rail Elementary, had gone through "military shooting drills" with veterans who fought in Iraq, The Guardian reported. Seeing the shooting unfold, Giamanco "pursued" gunman Griffin J. John II, his mother, Kenda Freeman, told CBS News . Freeman said the experience has left her son traumatized. "I told him he was a hero, he did what he had to do, and that he did the right thing, and that I was proud of him and that he was a hero and he saved a lot of lives." "Kaylub knew something was not right, so he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school," Freeman said. "He crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army crawled through the window." Giamanco, who legally owns and carries his weapon, doesn't wish to speak about the school shooting because he feels "riddled with guilt" for not being able to save more lives, his brother, Kyle Giamanco, told the New York Post . A teacher in the classroom had already thrown her cellphone at John, tackled him and fought him, police said. She was not injured. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said her actions likely prevented more bloodshed. Giamanco then fired at John multiple times with a legally owned .40-caliber pistol, killing him just before police arrived, officials said. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised the Bend resident at a press conference, without naming him, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Addressing him directly, she acknowledged the toll it had taken on him. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well." "I don't think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage," Krantz said Friday, speaking about the teacher and the man who shot the gunman. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. And the quick thinking to … follow someone into the school is incredible, and undoubtedly saved people." Gun used 'purchased as a birthday gift' The gun used by the 16-year-old shooter Griffin J. John II was purchased by his mother as a birthday gift, according to reports. The Maverick 12-gauge shotgun was purchased legally in August 2026 by the mother of the gunman who carried out the shooting, and given to him for recreational use, sources told CBS News . On Friday, two senior law enforcement officials told NBC News that John's mother bought the shotgun and has been cooperating with investigators. The shooter killed Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old student, and Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher from Bend, along with two other children aged 8 and 11 on Thursday. Police said all of the shots were fired inside a single special needs classroom. In an interview with CNN on Sunday, John's mother said that "there were no warning signs" and wouldn't comment on how her son got access to the gun used in the shooting. Schools remain closed Schools across Bend., Ore., will stay closed Monday and Tuesday as the community mourns four people killed on Thursday, when police say a 16-year-old former student opened fire in a special education classroom. Students return Wednesday on an early-release schedule, and Silver Rail will remain closed until further notice, the Bend Bulletin reported . In a statement, Lambert's family described her as a native central Oregonian who grew up in Bend and had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. "Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in," the statement continued. "Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher. … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. … She was funny and opinionated and she lit up the room." Megan Lambert, 25, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., was killed in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed in Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore. Bend Police Department The shooter was identified as Griffin J. John II. He was a former student at the school who had received special ed services, according to Bend-La Pine School Superintendent Steven Cook. The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians confirmed Saturday that John was an enrolled member, NBC News reported . A 7-year-old girl who received lifesaving care at the scene was in serious but stable condition at Oregon Health & Science University, police said. A 54-year-old teacher, Becky Drury of Bend, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and was being treated at St. Charles Bend. Her family allowed police to release her name. Becky Drury, 54, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, was injured in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department According to a Facebook post from her mother-in-law, Drury has already had surgery to repair significant damage to her left arm and will need more surgeries in the future. She also suffered injuries to her right hand, but none of her wounds are believed to be life-threatening. "The good news is she will be ok and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives," the post read. Her husband, Will Drury, said her left arm "took a lot of damage" and that her right hand also needed surgery, CNN reported . The two other children killed, both boys, were 8 and 11. Their families asked police not to release their names. Other than John's past association with the school, police did not share any information on the potential motive behind the shooting. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." How the shooting unfolded Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday. AP Photo/Haven Daley Krantz provided new details about what happened in the chaotic few minutes from when John first opened fire outside the school to when he was killed. According to Krantz, John approached the school at approximately 12:58 p.m. on foot before throwing his gun over an exterior fence and climbing onto the school's property. A driver in a red pickup truck spotted John and "verbally confronted" him from inside their vehicle. John fired at least three rounds at the truck before heading inside. The driver, who was unhurt, quickly called 911 to alert police. John then walked around the outside of the school and fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of an exterior door to gain access to the school. He then turned left into a special education classroom and immediately began firing. In total, John fired as many as 15 rounds, Krantz said. Officers arrived at the scene within three minutes of the first 911 call. "Seconds later, officers reported the suspect had been shot and killed, possibly by a bystander," police wrote in an incident report on Thursday. Officers then cleared the school, and all students and staff were transported to a nearby church for reunification with families and guardians. According to Krantz, John was carrying an additional 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. Police had initially said that the three children who were killed and the one who was injured were the only students in the classroom at the time of the shooting. But on Monday, they confirmed that a fifth student had been present. That student was "physically unharmed by the assailant," a spokesman for the school district told the Oregonian . A fourth adult, a special education staff member who was also unharmed, was also in the room, police said. Investigators have searched John's home and plan to keep control of the school until at least Tuesday to finish collecting evidence, police said. They are asking anyone with video of a teenage boy in black clothing and a black backpack near Third Street, Brosterhous Road or the school between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. Thursday to submit it. The FBI has set up a tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI and fbi.gov/silverrailschool . 'Rhoam was so so strong' People leave a family reunification area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline Rhoam Summer's parents, Kelik and Lillian, released a new statement on Monday through their attorneys providing more details on who he was and how best to honor his memory. "Rhoam was so so strong. The day he was born, his father gave him his first sink bath at the hospital. In the sink, Rhoam grabbed his dad's hands and pulled himself up with his own strength. He climbed a ladder (3 step stool) when he was just 6 months old. He never stopped moving. He never stopped climbing. He could do anything," they wrote in the statement shared by the law firm Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss. A GoFundMe set up by friends of the family, one of 10 fundraisers that the site has verified to support those connected to the shooting, has raised more than $187,000 as of Tuesday. In their statement, the Summers said another way to remember Rhoam is to embody the spirit he lived with. "If people want to memorialize our little Rhoam, we request you draw. Sharks, dinosaurs, monsters... Rhoam loved to tell stories of creatures with big teeth who needed understanding and friendship. Please make art for him. Draw or paint. Use your hands if you can. Get messy," they wrote. Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss is one of three law firms the Summers have reportedly hired to "preserve and protect Rhoam's memory and investigate possible legal claims arising from the mass school shooting," according to the Salem Statesman Journal . "Senseless, barbaric, and depraved? Yes. But was it foreseeable and thus preventable?" Tim Williams, cocounsel on the investigation, told the paper. "That's what we will find out. While law enforcement handles the criminal prosecution, we will be investigating any systemic failures that may have allowed this tragedy to happen. We are committed to holding all responsible parties accountable to ensure a tragedy like this never happens again and justice is done in Rhoam's name." Alberta separatists rallied ahead of the vote in the provincial capital of Edmonton (Megan Albu) Canada's province of Alberta rejected a plan to hold a binding independence referendum, results showed Tuesday, a win for unity as the country faces worsening ties with the United States. Public broadcaster CBC and leading private network CTV projected a clear win for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76 percent support for Alberta remaining in Canada with nearly 45 percent of ballots counted. Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the result and said Albertans had made a "clear choice" in favor of unity. "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other," he said in a statement on X. Carney, who grew up in Alberta, urged the province to reject separatism and argued that Canada needed stability as it confronted US President Donald Trump's trade war and annexation threats. A sombre mood took over the restaurant in the provincial capital Edmonton where a leading separatist group watched the returns. Jeffrey Rath, a top leader of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project, told reporters his push for independence will "absolutely" continue, despite the result from Monday's vote. "As far as I'm concerned we've already won. We've created a massive movement in this province," Rath said. "We've been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence and we're continuing to move forward." Separatist supporter Roger Hodkinson, an 82-year-old retired doctor, told AFP "this movement is not going to stop." Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative who opposed independence, praised the "widespread support for remaining in Canada" on Tuesday. Smith, who called the referendum, said a win for the federalists would settle the secession issue, which has divided the province. Thomas Lukaszuk, who leads the pro-unity group Forever Canadian, said it was "amazing to see the enthusiasm and resolve among Canadians." - Foreign influence? - Alberta has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, and much of the separatist momentum has been driven by anger over oil industry management. Smith blamed Carney's predecessor Justin Trudeau for igniting the separatist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda. Alberta's independence push has also drawn sustained interest from Trump allies. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States. Elon Musk, the world's richest person and a top Trump supporter, posted on X this month that Alberta "should separate." Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project also held meetings at the US State Department, while separatists received advice from Republican political operatives. - 'Rash decisions' - Carney has worked to improve relations between the province and Ottawa since taking office last year. He has partnered with Smith on advancing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas, a project considered a nonstarter during Trudeau's tenure. item.title: Nearly $1 million in sports and Pokémon cards stolen from FedEx truck
item.description:

Nearly $1 million worth of sports and Pokémon trading cards were stolen from a FedEx truck last week, police in California said Monday. (David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty) Thieves made off with nearly $1 million in sports, Pokémon and other trading cards swiped from a FedEx truck in Southern California last week, police said Monday. Officers responded to a trading card authentication company Tuesday about the theft of an estimated $963,000 worth of cards from a FedEx truck, Santa Ana police spokesperson Natalie Garcia said by email. The theft included two pallets of cards and a third that was “disrupted,” she said. The location of the report was Professional Sports Authenticator in the city of Santa Ana, about 33 miles southeast of Los Angeles. The company bills itself on its website as “the leading third-party authentication and grading service” and says it can sell customers’ cards online for a percentage of the selling price to “turn cards into currency.” Nick Andrews, known on social media as the Boston Card Hunter, said on X that there are multiple victims of the theft, one of whom he said lost $500,000 worth of cards. When all is said and done, he said, the heist could be one of the biggest in trading card history. He has compiled a list of cards claimed to have been taken in the theft that numbered as high as 383 on Monday evening. Among them, as the video game news site IGN noted , were a 1995 Upper Deck 23K Gold Michael Jordan card and a 2024 One Piece Simplified Chinese 1st Anniversary Set Nami. Card trader Sky-B, who said he wants to be referred to only under that moniker, discussed cards he said he lost in the theft in a video on YouTube on Monday. “These were 104 cards that I’ve accumulated over two years,” he said. “There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again. And, honestly, that’s what hurts the most — outside of obviously being absolutely financially destroyed here.” He said the missing cards were dropped off at Professional Sports Authenticator, where they were certified and started their journey back to him in Michigan before he discovered they had been stolen. Sky-B said he paid $8,000 in grading fees and lamented that he would be out the likely increased value that the grading added to his cards, which he said were insured up to $156,000 — below their likely market value. A company spokesperson said in an email that grading fees would be returned, along with the fair market value of the cards involved. In a statement, the company said it is working with investigators and has deactivated the stolen cards’ certificates. “We have deactivated the certificates for the stolen items and notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items,” a Professional Sports Authenticator spokesperson said. FedEx said in a statement that getting to the bottom of the theft is paramount. “The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation,” it said. Garcia, the police spokesperson, said the value of the stolen goods could rise. “It remains an open case,” she said, “and we have not made any arrests or recovered any stolen goods.” In 2024, a FedEx shipment of 54 vintage baseball cards worth $2.1 million was successfully delivered to a Best Western in Strongsville, Ohio, for a sports card conference, but it was stolen by a hotel employee who was sentenced to four to six years in prison , prosecutors in nearby Cleveland said. Attorneys for the Wiley family said that the adults were accused of stealing diapers. WATN - PHOTO: Photos of Kohen Wiley are shown during a press event in Senatobia, Mississippi, June 22, 2026. Officers attempted to stop the vehicle, with one opening fire when the driver allegedly drove toward them, the bureau said. The child was killed and an adult critically injured, officials said. "How can anyone accept that conclusion when Kohen’s family and the public still have not been allowed to see the body-camera footage?" Crump added.
